body.text: As North Korea’s military cooperation with Russia has continued throughout 2026, numerous assessments have suggested that this is leading to visible improvement in the domestic economic situation. For example, a Wall Street Journal article argued in June that North Korea is the “world’s most surprising economic success story.” In addition to Pyongyang’s cooperation with Moscow, continued economic engagement with China alongside illicit activities such as cybertheft and sanctions violations are seen as having contributed to this apparent economic revival.
To what extent, however, does the available economic data support this view?

According to the most recent data released by the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, 2025 did indeed see a continuation of the post-COVID recovery of North Korea’s external trade. North Korea’s total trade in 2025 amounted to $3.13 billion, compared to $2.70 billion in 2024, and $2.77 billion in 2024. However, this increase in external trade was accompanied by an increasingly sizeable deficit, as imports outstripped exports. This deficit has grown from $550 million in 2021 to $2.2 billion in 2025.
The first nine months of 2026 have seen a further increase in trade, with imports rising by 12.1 percent over the same period in 2025, and exports by a significant 50.5 percent.

Despite this ongoing recovery, North Korea’s external trade still falls far short of the levels seen a decade ago, when the country was a key exporter of mineral resources to China’s booming economy. Indeed, in 2016, North Korean exports had amounted to $2.8 billion, nearly six times the 2025 figure.
China remains by far North Korea’s dominant trading partner, accounting for 98.2 percent of the country’s external trade in 2025.
A key absence in KOTRA’s recent data, however, are the statistics relating to North Korea-Russia trade. Russia stopped publishing these statistics following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

As argued in a 2025 Korea Development Institute report, while the scale is not large, trade with Russia has included some strategically important goods, most notably Russian exports of refined petroleum productions, which between 2018 and 2020 amounted to a value of $54.9 billion. Russia has also been a key supplier of wheat and other food products, as well as machinery and components used in power-generation.
It is also likely that North Korea has received cash payments or payments-in-kind for its dispatch of troops and labor as well as exports of military materiel to Russia.

South Korea’s Institute for National Security Strategy has estimated the value of such exports between August 2023 and December 2025 at between $7.67 billion and $14.4 billion, although this does not necessarily equate to actual payments received by Pyongyang. Such estimates are fraught with methodological difficulties and problematic assumptions, however, and should be treated with a considerable degree of caution. The same can be said for proceeds from cybercrime, which are extremely difficult to calculate.
How then can the impact of the renewed North Korea-Russian cooperation be more reliably assessed?

Researchers at the Korea Development Institute have analyzed satellite pictures of North Korean light emissions as a proxy of economic activity. This analysis shows that regions with a high concentration of heavy industries and defense-related production have shown higher light emissions following the deepening of relations between Pyongyang and Moscow than those without such industries. Enterprises in transport machinery, including shipbuilding and railway equipment, have also seen greater light intensity.

Conversely, industries closely related to the civilian economy (food processing, tobacco, beverages and alcoholic drinks, general food products, and animal feed) have not seen a significant improvement in electricity conditions.

This finding is backed up by the Bank of Korea’s estimates of North Korean economic growth, which calculates that in 2024, the heavy industrial sector saw 10.7 percent annual growth along with 8.8 percent growth in mining compared to the previous year, whereas light industry actually saw a contraction of 0.7 percent, and agriculture, forestry, and fishing a decline of 1.9 percent.

Further insights into the state of the North Korean economy can be gained from examining the domestic policy priorities. Since January 2024, a key priority has been the so-called “20 x 10 Regional Development Policy,” based on the goal of constructing factories in 20 cities/counties every year for ten years. The policy reflects the seemingly belated recognition that a key shortcoming in North Korean economic development has been not just its urban bias, but specifically its Pyongyang-centric nature.

The policy is aimed developing light industry, including food processing, clothing, and everyday consumer goods, though it has subsequently been expanded to include the building of hospitals, cultural and service facilities, and grain-management infrastructure.

According to a report by the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy, satellite analysis suggests that there has been a significant increase in nighttime luminosity (24 percent) in areas prioritized by the policy. It is not clear, however, whether this constitutes a diversion of resources, including energy, from areas not targeted. Indeed, as noted above, North Korea’s recent growth has more broadly been concentrated in the heavy industries and defense sector.

Furthermore, the challenges faced by the 20 x 10 policy are obvious. Observers have noted that there is a large gap between the construction of facilities and the subsequent maintenance of production, given the need for reliable electricity, raw materials, transport, skilled workers, maintenance, and access to consumers. There have also reportedly been problems related to quality, with Kim Jong Un himself criticizing the poor construction of factories.

The policy also seems extraordinarily inefficient, as it is by no means clear that a geographically small country with a moderately sized population needs so many factories producing consumer goods, given the limited economies of scale involved.

As such, while the narrative of a booming North Korean economy has some degree of truth to it, this growth appears to be largely limited to the heavy industries and defense sectors, with weak linkages to the civilian livelihoods. Efforts by the North Korean state to move away from the urban-centered industrialization model of the past face significant hurdles in the form of lack of resources as well as the dominance of the security imperative over what would otherwise be more rational economic policies.

The flip side of this argument, however, is that North Korea’s current geopolitical alignments may not provide a permanent resolution to its longstanding developmental challenges. Some kind of rapprochement with the United States may still remain a precondition for the broader normalization of the country’s external economic relations.
